title: The Giant in the Workshop: Florence, 1494–1504
subtitle: The French entry, Savonarola, and Michelangelo's David, Florence, 1494–1504
intro: In November 1494 a French army walked into Florence, the Medici family rode out of it, and a Dominican friar from Ferrara found that the city believed he had foretold it all. Ten years later a seventeen-foot marble nude, carved by a twenty-nine-year-old sculptor from a block that had lain spoiled in the cathedral yard for decades, was hauled through the same streets and set up at the door of the government palace. This chapter lays the eyes of that decade side by side: the years of the friar's republic, its bonfires and its violent end, and the years when the restored republic commissioned the David and set Leonardo and Michelangelo to paint rival battles in its council hall.

The backbone is the diary of Luca Landucci, an apothecary whose shop stood at the corner of the Tornaquinci, a few minutes' walk from both the Piazza and San Marco. He wrote short dated notes for half a century: grain prices, executions, sermons, weather, processions. He believed in Savonarola, watched him burn, and six years later noted the hour the marble giant left the cathedral workshop and the night someone threw stones at it. Around him stand voices of very different kinds: the friar's own dated sermons; the memoirs of Philippe de Commynes, the French king's envoy who visited Savonarola in his convent; Michelangelo's letters; Leonardo's dated notes; Machiavelli's letters and the chancery he joined weeks after the execution; a chancery clerk's marginal note in a copy of Cicero; the brother of Botticelli; and the minutes of a committee of artists.

Much of this record is not diary in the strict sense. The committee of 25 January 1504 survives as a notarial minute in the archive of the Opera of Santa Maria del Fiore, so it appears here as an institutional eye; the herald Francesco Filarete and the architect Giuliano da Sangallo are known chiefly through what that minute records them saying. Commynes wrote his memoirs after the events. Simone Filipepi's chronicle survives only in extracts. Each eye's form tag says plainly what kind of document it is.

The two halves of the decade belong together. The bonfires of 1497 and 1498 burned paintings, mirrors, lutes and books in the same Piazza where the David was later placed, and the republic that the friar's preaching helped found in 1494, with its Great Council and its huge new hall, is the republic that in 1504 wanted a giant at its door and battle scenes on its walls. The committee debated whether the statue should replace Donatello's Judith; the herald argued that Judith, a woman killing a man, had brought the city bad luck. In the end the David took Judith's place on the platform in front of the palace.

Savonarola's death on 23 May 1498 is treated here soberly: what Landucci and others wrote, and how the city changed its mind. Where later stories have grown around the David (Vasari's tale of the gonfaloniere and the nose, the claim that Botticelli burned his own paintings), they are flagged as later claims and not presented as part of the dated record.
calendar_note: Florence counted the new year from the Incarnation, 25 March (stile fiorentino), so any document dated between 1 January and 24 March carries the previous year's number. Landucci's Carnival bonfire 'of 27 February 1497' is 27 February 1498 in modern reckoning; the committee on the David met on 25 January 1503 by Florentine count, which is 25 January 1504; Machiavelli's letter on Savonarola's sermons is dated 9 March 1497 in the Florentine style and belongs to 1498; and Botticelli's inscription on the Mystic Nativity, 'at the end of the year 1500', could by Florentine count fall as late as March 1501. All dates here are given in the Julian calendar then in use (ten days behind the Gregorian after 1500), with the year begun on 1 January. Florentines also counted hours from sunset, so Landucci's giant leaving the workshop 'at 24 o'clock' means at nightfall, and its arrival in the Piazza 'at 12 o'clock' means about eight in the morning, twelve hours after the previous sunset. Weekdays given in the sources have been checked against the Julian calendar; Leonardo's note that his father died on 'Wednesday' 9 July 1504 does not match, since that day was a Tuesday.

eyes.name: Luca Landucci
eyes.role: Apothecary with a shop at the Canto de' Tornaquinci, about 58 in 1494 and 68 in 1504; a devout follower of Savonarola
eyes.side: Florence; a shopkeeping citizen, piagnone in sympathy
eyes.where: His spice shop near the Strozzi palace, between the Piazza della Signoria and San Marco
eyes.authenticity: The diary (1450–1516, continued by another hand to 1542) survives in manuscript and was edited by Iodoco Del Badia (Florence, Sansoni, 1883); English translation by Alice de Rosen Jervis, A Florentine Diary from 1450 to 1516 (London, 1927). Entries are short, dated, and written close to the events, though some passages were evidently written up a little later.
eyes.bio: Landucci recorded the price of grain beside sermons and executions, which makes his diary the steadiest civic eye of the decade. He believed in the friar's prophecies, recorded the bonfires with approval, and watched the execution, then noted soberly how many lost faith afterwards. His entry on the moving of the marble giant is the fullest eyewitness account of the David's journey.

sources.title: Diario fiorentino dal 1450 al 1516, ed. I. Del Badia (1883), full text at Internet Archive

eyes.name: Girolamo Savonarola
eyes.role: Dominican friar from Ferrara, prior of San Marco; the city's leading preacher, aged 42 in 1494
eyes.side: Florence; the piagnoni (his followers) against the Medici party and the Compagnacci
eyes.where: The convent of San Marco and the pulpit of Santa Maria del Fiore
eyes.form: dated sermons (taken down by listeners) and letters
eyes.authenticity: His sermons survive mostly as transcriptions made by listeners, notably the notary Lorenzo Violi, and were printed in his lifetime and after; they are dated by the liturgical day on which they were preached. Prison writings (the meditations on Psalms 50 and 30) survive in early printings. His trial confessions were edited by his enemies and are not treated here as his own voice.
eyes.bio: Savonarola read the French invasion as the sword he had predicted and preached a reformed, godly republic with a Great Council. His boys' brigades collected 'vanities' for the Carnival bonfires of 1497 and 1498. Excommunicated in 1497, he kept preaching until March 1498, and after the failed ordeal by fire and the assault on San Marco he was tried and executed.

sources.title: P. Villari, Life and Times of Girolamo Savonarola, vol. 2 (PDF)

eyes.name: Philippe de Commynes
eyes.role: Lord of Argenton, counsellor of Charles VIII, French ambassador at Venice 1494–95
eyes.where: Venice during the French entry into Florence; in Florence in June 1495 on his way to rejoin the king
eyes.authenticity: Books VII–VIII of the Mémoires, on the Italian expedition, were written c. 1495–98 and printed in 1528. Commynes writes from memory and to a purpose (the expedition as a work of God), but his visit to Savonarola is first-hand. English translation by A. R. Scoble (1855–56), on Project Gutenberg.
eyes.bio: A shrewd diplomat who distrusted most prophets, Commynes nonetheless judged Savonarola a sincere and good man and took his warnings seriously. He gives the French side of the 1494 entry and the clearest outside account of the friar's influence over the king.

sources.title: The Memoirs of Philip de Commines, vol. 2 (Scoble trans.), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
eyes.role: Sculptor, 19 in 1494, 26 when he took the David contract, 29 at its unveiling
eyes.side: Florence; formerly of Lorenzo de' Medici's household
eyes.where: Fled to Venice and Bologna in 1494; Rome 1496–1501; the Opera's walled workshop beside the cathedral 1501–04
eyes.authenticity: His letters survive in the Archivio Buonarroti (Casa Buonarroti, Florence); the earliest, of 2 July 1496, is to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici. Condivi's Life (1553) and Vasari's Lives (1550, 1568) add stories told decades later; those are flagged where used.
eyes.bio: Michelangelo left Florence before the French arrived and spent the friar's years mostly in Bologna and Rome, where he made the Bacchus and the Pietà. He came home in 1501 to the block called 'the Giant' and worked on it behind walls for over two years. In 1504 he was given the second battle painting for the council hall, opposite Leonardo.

sources.title: Casa Buonarroti / Google Arts & Culture: letter to his father (Archivio Buonarroti IV 1)

eyes.name: Leonardo da Vinci
eyes.role: Painter and engineer, 42 in 1494; in Milan until December 1499, back in Florence from 1500
eyes.side: Milan (Sforza court), then the Florentine republic; briefly Cesare Borgia's engineer (1502–03)
eyes.where: Milan; then Florence, with a studio in the Sala del Papa at Santa Maria Novella from late 1503

waypoints.label: Sala del Papa, S. Maria Novella, 1503–05

eyes.vantage_label: the rival master on the committee
eyes.authenticity: Dated notes survive in the Codex Atlanticus and Codex Arundel, the Paris manuscripts and the Madrid codices; the Signoria's records of his council-hall commission are edited in Richter's Literary Works. His own dates are usually exact, though he occasionally slips (the weekday of his father's death).
eyes.bio: Leonardo arrived back in Florence after the fall of his Milanese patron and found a city at war with Pisa and a young sculptor famous for a marble he had once been considered for. He sat on the David committee, sketched the statue, and took the commission for the Battle of Anghiari. His notes are terse and personal: a death, an hour, a storm.

eyes.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
eyes.role: Young Florentine of a modest family, 29 in 1498; from June 1498 secretary of the Second Chancery and of the Ten of War
eyes.where: Palazzo della Signoria, and on missions abroad
eyes.authenticity: The letter to Ricciardo Becchi survives and is dated 9 March 1497 (Florentine style). His chancery papers survive in the Archivio di Stato di Florence. The Decennale primo, a verse chronicle of 1494–1504, was printed in 1506.
eyes.bio: Machiavelli heard Savonarola in March 1498 and described him to a friend in Rome as a politician adapting his message to the moment. Weeks after the execution he entered the chancery of the new regime, and by 1504 he was close to the gonfaloniere Soderini and involved in the council-hall commissions.

eyes.name: Agostino Vespucci
eyes.role: Chancery clerk and assistant to Machiavelli; cousin of the navigator Amerigo Vespucci
eyes.authenticity: His marginal note dated 'October 1503' in a 1477 Bologna edition of Cicero's Epistulae ad familiares was found by Armin Schlechter at Heidelberg University Library and published in 2005/2008. His account of the battle of Anghiari, written out for Leonardo, survives in the Codex Atlanticus; his letters to Machiavelli survive in the Machiavelli papers.
eyes.bio: Agostino's few words in a book margin are the only contemporary document that ties Leonardo's portrait to Lisa del Giocondo and that dates it, and they show the clerk already knew Leonardo was to paint the council hall. He was the link between the chancery's writers and the painter.

eyes.name: Sandro Botticelli
eyes.role: Painter, about 49 in 1494; long associated with the Medici, later drawn to Savonarola's preaching
eyes.side: Florence; Medici clientele, then piagnone sympathies
eyes.where: His house and shop in the Ognissanti quarter
eyes.form: inscription on a painting and civic records
eyes.authenticity: Botticelli left no diary or letters; his voice survives in the Greek inscription on the Mystic Nativity (National Gallery, London, NG1034), in the David committee minute, and through his brother Simone's chronicle. Vasari's statement that he was a fervent piagnone and gave up painting is a later claim and is treated as such.
eyes.bio: The painter of the Birth of Venus served as the forwarding address for the young Michelangelo's first surviving letter. In 1500 or early 1501 he inscribed his Nativity with a reading of 'the troubles of Italy' through the Book of Revelation, and in January 1504 he sat on the David committee.

eyes.name: Simone Filipepi
eyes.role: Botticelli's elder brother, a convinced follower of Savonarola who kept a chronicle
eyes.vantage_label: the painter's brother, keeping the friar's memory
eyes.authenticity: Only extracts of Simone's chronicle survive, in a Vatican manuscript published by Villari and Casanova (Scelta di prediche e scritti di fra Girolamo Savonarola, 1898). The dating of individual notes rests on Simone's own headings.
eyes.bio: Simone recorded what the friar's enemies said after his death, including a conversation in Botticelli's house with Doffo Spini, a leader of the Compagnacci. His chronicle is the main evidence for Botticelli's own sympathies.

sources.title: P. Villari, Life and Times of Girolamo Savonarola (PDF), with discussion of Filipepi

eyes.name: The Operai of Santa Maria del Fiore (minute books)
eyes.role: The board of works of Florence Cathedral, under the Arte della Lana; owner of the marble block
eyes.side: Florence; the cathedral works and the wool guild
eyes.where: The Opera's offices and yard beside the cathedral
eyes.vantage_label: the institution that owned the block
eyes.authenticity: The deliberations, the contract of 16 August 1501 and the minute of the 25 January 1504 meeting survive in the Archivio dell'Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore and were printed by Gaye (Carteggio inedito, 1840) and many since. The minute was exhibited at the Museo dell'Opera in 2019.
eyes.bio: The Operai had owned a damaged colossal block since the 1460s. Their dry Latin minutes record the decision to stand it up, the contract with Michelangelo, his first blows, and the meeting of artists called to decide where the finished statue should go.

sources.title: Affaritaliani: the 25 January 1504 minute exhibited at the Museo dell'Opera (2019)
Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore: Michelangelo and the Cathedral

eyes.name: Francesco di Lorenzo Filarete
eyes.role: First herald of the Signoria, master of ceremonies of the palace
eyes.vantage_label: the herald who wanted Judith gone
eyes.authenticity: His opinion is recorded in the Opera's minute of 25 January 1504. He also kept, with his successor Angelo Manfidi, a ceremonial book of the palace (ed. R. Trexler, 1978), not used for dated entries here.
eyes.bio: As the official responsible for ceremonies on the palace platform, Filarete spoke first at the committee. He argued that Donatello's Judith, a woman killing a man and set up under an evil star, was an unlucky emblem and that the giant should replace her.

sources.title: Affaritaliani: report of the committee opinions

eyes.name: Giuliano da Sangallo
eyes.role: Architect and engineer, about 60 in 1504; formerly Lorenzo de' Medici's architect
eyes.side: Florence; Medici-trained, working for the republic
eyes.where: Florence; the Piazza and the Loggia
eyes.vantage_label: the engineer who feared for the marble
eyes.authenticity: His opinion survives in the minute of 25 January 1504. Vasari credits him and his brother Antonio with the device used to move the statue; the Opera's own order of 11 June 1504 names Antonio da Sangallo and Simone del Pollaiolo (Cronaca) as in charge of the base.
eyes.bio: Giuliano spoke for the engineers: the marble was flawed and soft and would weather badly in the open, so the statue belonged under the Loggia's central arch, where people could walk around it. Leonardo backed him; the government did not.

sources.title: Affaritaliani: report of the committee opinions

entries.headline: The young sculptor slips away before the French arrive
entries.digest: With the French army approaching and Piero de' Medici's regime tottering, Michelangelo, who had lived in the Medici household, left Florence for Venice and then Bologna. Condivi later told the story of a lute-player's dream warning of Piero's fall; that is his biographer's tale, but the departure itself is secure, and Michelangelo spent the friar's years mostly away from the city.
entries.source_note: Condivi, Life of Michelangelo (1553); month from the sequence of events, not a dated letter.

entries.headline: From Venice, the envoy hears Florence has changed masters
entries.digest: As ambassador at Venice, Commynes followed the king's march by letters. He later set down, in two chapters of his memoirs, how the king came from Pisa toward Florence, how Piero de' Medici, who had handed over the Florentine fortresses, was driven out of his own city, and how the king then made his entry. His view was a Frenchman's at a distance, assembled from dispatches.
entries.source_note: Commynes, Mémoires, Book VII, chs. X–XI (Scoble trans., Project Gutenberg vol. 2); written later.

entries.place: Florence, the streets near the Piazza
entries.headline: Piero de' Medici flees by the San Gallo gate
entries.digest: Landucci recorded the Sunday when Piero de' Medici, back in the city after yielding the fortresses to the French king, was refused at the government palace while the city rose against him. Piero left by the San Gallo gate, his brothers soon following, and Medici property was plundered. The diarist set it down in the same plain hand he used for grain prices.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 9 Nov 1494 (fetched Italian text).

entries.place: Florence, Porta San Frediano to the Duomo
entries.headline: Charles VIII rides into Florence at the 22nd hour
entries.digest: The French king entered late in the afternoon, at about the 22nd hour, under a canopy, armed, lance on thigh, with a vast train of soldiers. Landucci described the crowds, the decorations, and the king going to the cathedral and then to lodge in the Medici palace. He noted the city's fear as well as its show.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 17 Nov 1494.

entries.headline: The king leaves after dinner, to everyone's relief
entries.digest: After the treaty had been sworn at Santa Maria del Fiore on 26 November, the king left Florence after his midday meal and lodged at the Certosa. Landucci's entry carries the relief of a city that had spent eleven days with a foreign army in its houses.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entries of 26 and 28 Nov 1494.

entries.headline: The friar preaches a new government for the city
entries.digest: In his Advent sermons on the prophet Haggai, Savonarola turned from prophecy to constitution, urging a broad council of citizens on the Venetian model and a city ruled by Christ. Within days the Great Council was voted, and the old hall of the palace soon had to be replaced by a huge new one for it, the hall Leonardo and Michelangelo would be asked to paint ten years later.
entries.source_note: Prediche sopra Aggeo (Advent 1494); day of the sermon on the Great Council as commonly cited; the law creating the Council passed 22–23 Dec 1494.

entries.headline: Fra Girolamo preaches, and wants no women present
entries.digest: Landucci noted that on this Sunday the friar preached and would not have women in the congregation. The short entry is typical of how closely the diarist followed every sermon of these weeks, when the new regime and its laws were being preached into being.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 28 Dec 1494.

entries.headline: The French envoy calls on the friar
entries.digest: Passing through Florence to rejoin the retreating king, Commynes went with the king's steward to see Savonarola in his convent. The friar told him the king would meet great danger on the road home but would come through it, and that God would punish him for letting his soldiers plunder and for not restoring Florence's towns. Commynes judged him a good man and later saw his words fulfilled at Fornovo.
entries.source_note: Commynes, Mémoires, Book VIII, ch. III (Scoble trans.); month inferred from the king's route north, June 1495.

entries.headline: Fra Girolamo goes to speak with the king
entries.digest: Landucci recorded that the friar went to meet Charles VIII at Poggibonsi as the French army came back north. The city feared the king would enter Florence again; Savonarola's mission was to keep him away and to warn him to keep his promises.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 17 June 1495.

entries.headline: First surviving letter, sent care of Botticelli
entries.digest: Writing from Rome a week after arriving, Michelangelo reported to his patron Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici that he had presented his letters to Cardinal Riario, been shown the cardinal's antiquities, and bought marble to begin a figure. The dealer who had sold his sleeping Cupid as an antique would not give it back. The letter was addressed under cover to Sandro Botticelli in Florence, who served as go-between.
entries.source_note: Archivio Buonarroti; Ramsden, Letters of Michelangelo, no. 1. Date per the letter; the cover addressed to Botticelli as given in standard editions.

entries.headline: The first great bonfire of the vanities
entries.digest: Instead of the usual Carnival games, the friar's boys' companies, who had gone door to door collecting cards, dice, cosmetics, mirrors, lewd books and pictures, built a tiered pyramid of these things in the Piazza and set it alight after a procession. To his followers it was a purification of the city; to his enemies a show of tyranny by children.
entries.source_note: Schaff-Herzog, 'Savonarola'; History Hit, 'What was the Bonfire of the Vanities'. Carnival Tuesday 1497 fell on 7 Feb (Julian).

entries.headline: Pope Alexander VI excommunicates the friar
entries.digest: The brief of excommunication, dated in Rome on 12 May (often cited as 13 May), declared Savonarola suspect of heresy for defying orders to stop preaching. It was published in Florence's churches on 18 June. He answered with open letters arguing that an unjust excommunication was void.
entries.source_note: Schaff-Herzog, 'Savonarola' (12 May 1497); Italian Art Society (13 May).

entries.headline: The excommunicated friar returns to the cathedral pulpit
entries.digest: Landucci noted, under 11 February 1497 by Florentine count, that Fra Girolamo began preaching again in Santa Maria del Fiore, with the pews rebuilt, though he was excommunicated. On the following Sundays the diarist recorded smaller crowds, and remarked that a young notary was taking down every sermon word for word.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entries of 11, 15, 18, 25 Feb 1497 st. fl. (= 1498).

entries.headline: The second bonfire, guarded through the night
entries.digest: On the last day of Carnival the children, in four companies carrying crosses and olive branches, processed to the Piazza and burned a great pyre of vanities: figures of nudes, gaming boards, books judged heretical, mirrors and more. Armed men had guarded it overnight against the Compagnacci, and the friar blessed the crowd from a pulpit outside San Marco.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry 'E dì 27 di febraio, fu Carnasciale' (1497 st. fl. = 1498).

entries.headline: A cool young listener reports on the friar
entries.digest: Machiavelli wrote to Ricciardo Becchi, the Florentine envoy in Rome, describing the sermons he had just heard at San Marco. He thought the friar was shifting his message with the times, rallying his followers by painting his opponents as enemies of God, and colouring his claims to suit the political moment. It is the first surviving letter of Machiavelli's on politics.
entries.source_note: Letter to Ricciardo Becchi, 9 March 1497 st. fl.; Gilbert, Letters of Machiavelli; Chadwick, 'Machiavelli and Savonarola'.

entries.headline: The last sermon
entries.digest: Under mounting pressure from the pope and a Signoria no longer friendly, Savonarola preached for the last time. Days later a Franciscan challenged him to prove his teaching by walking through fire, and one of his own friars, Domenico da Pescia, accepted for him.
entries.source_note: Schaff-Herzog, 'Savonarola' (last sermon 18 March 1498).

entries.headline: After the failed ordeal, the city turns on San Marco
entries.digest: The ordeal by fire set for the day before had collapsed in argument while the crowd waited by a 50-braccia platform in the Piazza. On Palm Sunday a tumult broke out in the cathedral and spread; that evening San Marco was besieged and stormed and the friar taken. Landucci recorded the violence and the arrests.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entries of 7 and 8 April 1498.

entries.headline: The three friars are executed in the Piazza
entries.digest: Landucci wrote that on this Wednesday morning the 'sacrifice' of the three friars was carried out: Savonarola, Fra Domenico and Fra Silvestro were stripped of their orders on the platform, hanged, and their bodies burned; the ashes were thrown into the Arno. He had been a believer and he recorded, with evident sorrow, that many people lost their faith that day.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 23 May 1498 (fetched text, Italian).

entries.headline: The envoy blames the pope's malice
entries.digest: Commynes, by now back in France, gave a chapter of his memoirs to the burning, which he attributed to the malice of the pope and the friar's enemies in Florence. He still counted Savonarola a holy man whose prophecies about the king had come true.
entries.source_note: Commynes, Mémoires, Book VIII, ch. XXVI (chapter title); written after the event.

entries.headline: Machiavelli enters the chancery
entries.digest: Less than a month after the execution, the Great Council confirmed Machiavelli, 29 years old and without previous office, as head of the Second Chancery, in a purge that removed Savonarola's supporters from the government offices. He would serve the republic until 1512.
entries.source_note: Standard chronology of Machiavelli's career (Ridolfi); Chadwick notes his election after the execution.

entries.headline: 'The duke lost his state'
entries.digest: On the cover of a small notebook Leonardo listed in a few words the fate of his patron Ludovico Sforza, driven out by the French: the duke had lost his state, his goods and his liberty, and none of his works was finished for him. By December Leonardo had left Milan; by spring 1500 he was back in Florence.
entries.source_note: Paris, Institut de France, MS L, cover; note undated but written after the fall of Milan (Sept 1499).

entries.headline: The friar's enemy admits he found no fault
entries.digest: Simone recorded that Doffo Spini, a leader of the Compagnacci who had helped bring Savonarola to trial, was talking in Sandro's house and said that in the examinations they had found no sin in the friar, and had killed him to be rid of him. Sandro asked him directly why the friar had died so shamefully.
entries.source_note: Simone Filipepi, chronicle extracts (ed. Villari and Casanova, 1898); date as given in the extract, not independently checked.

entries.date_display: End of 1500 (Florentine count; possibly to March 1501)
entries.headline: A Nativity read through the Apocalypse
entries.digest: Botticelli painted a Nativity in which angels embrace men and small devils flee into the rocks, and wrote across the top in Greek that he painted it at the end of 1500 in the troubles of Italy, referring them to the eleventh chapter of Revelation. The invasions, the fall of Milan and the friar's death lie behind the picture's hope of a coming peace.
entries.source_note: National Gallery, London, NG1034, catalogue page (inscription and reading).

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: The Operai order the spoiled giant raised
entries.digest: The board of works decided that the colossal block, roughed out decades earlier by Agostino di Duccio and abandoned, should be stood upright so that masters could examine it and say whether it could be finished.
entries.source_note: Opera deliberation of 2 July 1501 (Latin), as cited in Wikipedia, David (Michelangelo).

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: A contract for 'the Giant'
entries.digest: The consuls of the Arte della Lana and the Operai contracted with Michelangelo to finish the marble figure called the Giant, badly blocked out by 'master Augustine', within two years from 1 September, at six florins a month.
entries.source_note: Contract of 16 Aug 1501, Archivio dell'Opera; Casa Buonarroti lecture text; Wikipedia.

entries.headline: Early on a Monday, he begins
entries.digest: A note added to the contract records that on 9 September Michelangelo had knocked off a 'knot' of marble on the figure's chest with one or two blows, and that early on the morning of Monday 13 September he began to work in earnest. A walled shelter was built around the block so he could carve unseen.
entries.source_note: Postil to the contract, Archivio dell'Opera; Wikipedia, David (Michelangelo).

entries.headline: A sheet with an arm, a slingshot and a rhyme
entries.digest: On a drawing sheet now in the Louvre, beside studies of an arm for the David, Michelangelo wrote a short line comparing David with his sling to himself with his bow, likely the sculptor's drill-bow. The jotting is undated but belongs to the years of the carving.
entries.quote: Davicte cholla fromba e io chollarcho
entries.source_note: Paris, Louvre, Département des Arts graphiques, inv. 714 recto; date by style and subject.

entries.headline: A gonfaloniere for life
entries.digest: Landucci recorded that the Great Council met and elected Piero di messer Tommaso Soderini gonfaloniere for life; Soderini entered the palace with the new Signoria on 1 November. The republic that would commission the David's site and the council-hall battles now had a permanent head.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entries of 22 Sept and 1 Nov 1502.

entries.headline: A note in the margin of Cicero
entries.digest: Reading a passage of Cicero on the painter Apelles, who left parts of his works unfinished, Agostino wrote beside it that Leonardo did the same in all his pictures, naming the head of Lisa del Giocondo and a St Anne, and added that Leonardo was to paint something in the great council hall, already agreed with the gonfaloniere. He dated the note October 1503.
entries.source_note: Heidelberg University Library, Cicero, Epistulae ad familiares (Bologna, 1477), margin; Heidelberg University press feature.

entries.headline: Keys to the Pope's Hall
entries.digest: The Signoria ordered that Leonardo be given the keys of the Sala del Papa at Santa Maria Novella, a large room where he could draw the cartoon for the council-hall battle. Records from early January show timber delivered for a scaffold in the room.
entries.source_note: Signoria records, ed. Richter, The Records 1494–1519, Part 6.

entries.headline: Writing out the battle for the painter
entries.digest: A long description of the battle of Anghiari, translated from a Latin history and written in Agostino's hand, survives among Leonardo's papers in the Codex Atlanticus. It gave the painter his cast of captains, the banners, the bridge, and a miracle of St Peter.
entries.source_note: Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Codex Atlanticus f. 74r-b (old 202a); attribution of the hand to Agostino Vespucci per modern scholarship.

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: Thirty masters are called to place the giant
entries.digest: With the statue nearly finished, the Operai summoned about thirty artists, artisans and officials to say where it should stand, since raising it to a buttress of the cathedral was no longer practical. The notary recorded each opinion in turn: the palace platform in place of Judith, the palace courtyard, the cathedral steps, or the Loggia.
entries.source_note: Minute of 25 Jan 1503 st. fl., Archivio dell'Opera (Gaye II); Affaritaliani report of the 2019 exhibition; Wikipedia.

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: The herald speaks first: move Judith
entries.digest: Speaking first, the herald named two places the government had in mind, the platform where Donatello's Judith stood or the centre of the palace courtyard. He preferred replacing Judith: a woman killing a man was a deadly sign, unfit for a city whose emblems were the cross and the lily, and the city had had nothing but misfortune since she was set up.
entries.source_note: Committee minute of 25 Jan 1504, as reported by Affaritaliani (2019).

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: Botticelli and Rosselli: the cathedral steps
entries.digest: Cosimo Rosselli proposed setting the statue by the steps of the cathedral, and Botticelli agreed, so that the giant would stand where the block had been meant to serve, near the church that owned it.
entries.source_note: Committee minute of 25 Jan 1504, as reported by Affaritaliani (2019).

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: Sangallo: shelter it under the Loggia
entries.digest: Giuliano da Sangallo argued for the central arch of the Loggia, set back so people could walk around it. The marble, he said, was imperfect and fragile from long exposure and should be kept out of the weather.
entries.source_note: Committee minute of 25 Jan 1504, as reported by Affaritaliani (2019).

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: Leonardo agrees: the Loggia, out of the way
entries.digest: Leonardo supported Sangallo: the Loggia, on the low wall where hangings were set, with suitable ornament, placed so as not to get in the way of the officials' ceremonies. Filippino Lippi is reported as saying the sculptor himself should be asked. The government in the end chose the herald's site.
entries.source_note: Committee minute of 25 Jan 1504 (Affaritaliani; Nicholl, Flights of the Mind). Filippino's view as commonly reported from the minute.

entries.place: Via de' Calzaiuoli to the Piazza
entries.headline: The machine that carried the giant
entries.digest: Vasari later credited Giuliano and his brother Antonio da Sangallo with the timber frame from which the statue hung, so that it rocked rather than bumped as it moved. The Opera's own records name Antonio and Simone del Pollaiolo (Cronaca) in charge of the move and the base; Giuliano's share rests on Vasari.
entries.source_note: Vasari, Life of Michelangelo (1568); Opera order of 11 June 1504 (Wikipedia, David).

entries.headline: The Anghiari contract is fixed
entries.digest: The Signoria set down terms for Leonardo's painting of the battle of Anghiari in the council hall: fifteen florins a month, the cartoon to be finished by the end of the following February, and the right to reclaim his pay if it was not. The deed was drawn up in the chancery where Machiavelli served.
entries.source_note: Deliberation of 4 May 1504, ed. Richter, Records 1494–1519, Part 6.

entries.headline: The secretary witnesses the painter's agreement
entries.digest: Machiavelli is named among those present at the drawing-up of the Anghiari agreement. The account of the 1440 battle supplied to Leonardo was copied out by his assistant Agostino Vespucci.
entries.source_note: Anghiari deliberation, 4 May 1504; Machiavelli's role as witness per standard accounts, not checked against the original.

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: The marble giant leaves the workshop at nightfall
entries.digest: Landucci wrote that the giant was taken out of the Opera at the 24th hour, at nightfall, and that the wall above the door had to be broken to let it pass. That night stones were thrown at it to damage it, and a guard had to be kept. He added, almost as an afterthought, that Michelangelo Buonarroti had made it.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 14 May 1504 (fetched Italian text).

entries.headline: Four days to cross half a mile
entries.digest: The statue travelled upright, slung inside a timber frame so its feet did not touch, on fourteen greased beams moved from back to front by more than forty men. Landucci noted it took four days to reach the Piazza, arriving on the 18th at the 12th hour, about eight in the morning.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), continuation of the 14 May 1504 entry.

entries.headline: The giant takes Judith's place
entries.digest: It took until 8 June, Landucci wrote, to set the giant on the platform in front of the palace, where Judith had been; Donatello's bronze had to be taken down and put inside the palace, on the ground. The herald's proposal had prevailed.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), 14 May 1504 entry, continuation.

entries.place: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore
entries.headline: A marble base for the giant
entries.digest: The Operai ordered Simone del Pollaiolo (Cronaca) and Antonio da Sangallo, who had overseen the transport, to make a base of marble for the statue on the palace platform.
entries.source_note: Opera order of 11 June 1504, as cited in Wikipedia, David (Michelangelo); Galleria Bazzanti.

entries.headline: 'My father' – a death noted twice
entries.digest: Leonardo wrote that on 9 July 1504, at the 7th hour, Ser Piero da Vinci, notary at the Palazzo del Podestà, his father, had died aged eighty, leaving ten sons and two daughters. He called the day Wednesday, though it was a Tuesday, and wrote a similar note again elsewhere. He was not among the legitimate heirs.
entries.source_note: Codex Arundel 272r and Codex Atlanticus; Discovering da Vinci, dated notes; weekday checked against the Julian calendar.

entries.headline: Work begins to turn the Arno – then stops
entries.digest: Landucci noted that work began to divert the Arno from Pisa toward Livorno, and then was abandoned. The scheme, intended to starve Pisa of its river, was promoted in the chancery where Machiavelli worked and had drawn Leonardo's interest the year before.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 22 Aug 1504.

entries.place: Florence, Sala dei Tintori at Sant'Onofrio
entries.headline: The second battle: Cascina
entries.digest: Soderini's government gave Michelangelo the other wall of the council hall, the battle of Cascina against Pisa, opposite Leonardo's Anghiari. He drew the cartoon in a room at the dyers' hospital from autumn 1504 into 1505, choosing the moment soldiers bathing in the Arno are surprised by the alarm. Neither painting was finished.
entries.source_note: Payments and paper deliveries of autumn 1504 as summarised in Casa Buonarroti lecture text ('Michelangelo politico'); exact contract date not established.

entries.headline: The giant finished and fully uncovered
entries.digest: On the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin, Landucci recorded that the giant in the Piazza was finished and uncovered entirely. Michelangelo had spent the summer completing details in place, with the gilded touches and the base now done.
entries.source_note: Landucci, Diario fiorentino, ed. Del Badia (1883), entry of 8 Sept 1504.

entries.headline: A verse chronicle of the ten years
entries.digest: Machiavelli dedicated his Decennale, a poem in terza rima on Italy's ten years from the French descent of 1494, to Alamanno Salviati. It reads the decade, the friar included, from the chancery's side, with Savonarola's light extinguished by a greater fire.
entries.source_note: Decennale primo, dedication dated November 1504; printed 1506.

entries.headline: Brush to wall, and the storm breaks
entries.digest: Leonardo noted that on Friday 6 June 1505, at the 13th hour, he began to paint in the palace. As he set down the brush the weather turned, the bell rang to call the men to court, the cartoon came loose, water spilled, and it rained hard until evening.
entries.source_note: Madrid, Biblioteca Nacional, Codex Madrid II f. 1r; weekday checked against the Julian calendar.

claims.claim: First bonfire of the vanities burns pictures, books, instruments and finery in the Piazza; Vasari's later claim that Botticelli and others burned their own paintings is unconfirmed by any contemporary record
claims.evidence: Contemporary accounts of the Carnival bonfire; Vasari, Lives (1550/1568) for the artists' claim

claims.claim: Second bonfire of the vanities, guarded overnight from the Compagnacci
claims.evidence: Landucci, entry of 27 Feb 1497 st. fl.

claims.claim: Mystic Nativity completed with its apocalyptic Greek inscription
Operai order the abandoned marble giant raised for inspection
Michelangelo contracted to finish 'the Giant' within two years
Begins carving the block that becomes David
Lisa del Giocondo's portrait recorded as in progress, and Leonardo's council-hall painting as agreed
claims.evidence: Agostino Vespucci's marginal note, Heidelberg incunabulum

claims.claim: Given the Sala del Papa as a studio for the battle cartoon
Committee of some thirty masters gives opinions on where to place the David; no single site agreed
claims.evidence: Opera minute of 25 Jan 1503 st. fl.

claims.claim: Terms fixed for the Battle of Anghiari in the Great Council hall
David moved from the Opera to the Piazza over four days; stoned by night
David set on the palace platform; Donatello's Judith removed indoors
David finished in place and fully uncovered
Commissioned to paint the Battle of Cascina opposite Leonardo; cartoon drawn 1504–05, fresco never begun
claims.evidence: Payments of autumn 1504; Casa Buonarroti summary

claims.claim: Vasari's anecdote that Soderini criticised the nose and Michelangelo pretended to fix it with marble dust: a later story, absent from any contemporary record
Begins painting the Anghiari battle on the council-hall wall

convergences.label: The French king enters Florence; the Medici are gone
convergences.note: Landucci watched the entry from the street and counted the hours; Commynes, in Venice, assembled it from dispatches as a stage in his king's providential march; Savonarola claimed it as the sword he had foretold; Michelangelo, of the Medici household, had already left.

convergences.label: The friar and the French on the road north
convergences.note: Within days of each other the friar spoke with the king at Poggibonsi and with the king's envoy at San Marco. Landucci recorded the mission as a civic service; Commynes recorded the prophecy and came to believe it.

convergences.label: The bonfires of the vanities
convergences.note: For the friar the bonfires purified the city; Landucci, a believer, described the processions approvingly and the night guard against the Compagnacci. Botticelli's part rests only on Vasari's later claim that he gave up painting and, in some tellings, burned work; no contemporary record confirms it.

convergences.label: The last sermons
convergences.note: Landucci counted thinning crowds at the Duomo; Machiavelli, at San Marco, heard a politician tailoring his message; the friar preached for the last time on 18 March.

convergences.label: The execution in the Piazza
convergences.note: Landucci watched with sorrow and recorded how many lost faith; Commynes, in France, blamed the pope; within a month Machiavelli held office in the new regime; a year and a half later Botticelli's brother recorded a leading enemy's admission that no fault had been found.

convergences.label: The committee on the David
convergences.note: In one room the herald argued from omens and civic symbols, Botticelli and Rosselli from the church that owned the marble, Sangallo from the stone's fragility, and Leonardo from ceremony and sight lines. The minute records disagreement; the government took the herald's site.

convergences.label: Anghiari commissioned while the giant is readied
convergences.note: The painter's contract, the secretary as witness and the clerk who wrote out the battle for him: the chancery made the council-hall commission as it made its war policy, ten days before the David left the workshop.

convergences.label: The four-day journey of the giant
convergences.note: Landucci gives the hours, the broken wall, the forty men and the stones; the Opera's records name the engineers; Vasari credits the Sangallo brothers with the hanging frame. Michelangelo left no letter about it.

convergences.label: The giant uncovered; the battles divided
convergences.note: Landucci noted the uncovering on the Virgin's feast; within weeks Michelangelo had the wall opposite Leonardo's in the council hall, setting the two artists side by side in the republic's largest room.

ties.note: Michelangelo's first surviving letter (Rome, 2 July 1496) went to his Medici patron under cover to Botticelli, who acted as go-between.
Simone was Sandro's elder brother; his chronicle records conversations in Sandro's house and is the main evidence for the painter's sympathy with the friar.
Landucci heard the friar preach for four years, recorded his sermons and bonfires as a believer, and watched him die.
Commynes visited the friar at San Marco in 1495 and judged him a good man whose prophecies about the king came true.
Machiavelli heard him in March 1498 and described him as adapting his message to the times; he entered office in the purge that followed his death.
Agostino Vespucci was Machiavelli's assistant in the chancery and wrote him lively letters during his missions.
Agostino wrote out the account of the battle of Anghiari that Leonardo used, and recorded the painter's portrait of Lisa del Giocondo in a margin.
Rivals in the same hall: Leonardo sat on the committee that judged where Michelangelo's statue should go, sketched it, and painted the battle facing Michelangelo's.
At the committee Leonardo explicitly agreed with Giuliano da Sangallo that the statue belonged in the Loggia.
The herald wanted the giant in Judith's place in the open; Sangallo wanted it sheltered in the Loggia. The herald's view prevailed.
The Operai contracted with Michelangelo, recorded his first blows and called the committee on his finished statue.
Landucci names Michelangelo Buonarroti as the maker of the giant in his entry of 14 May 1504.

threads_out.note: The Greek learning that shaped Lorenzo de' Medici's Florence, where the young Michelangelo grew up, came in large part from Byzantine scholars such as John Argyropoulos and Demetrius Chalcondyles, whose world ended with the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Agostino Vespucci, the chancery clerk who noted Leonardo's portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, was a cousin of Amerigo Vespucci, whose account of his voyages, the so-called Soderini letter, was addressed to the same gonfaloniere Piero Soderini who presided over the David and the council-hall battles.

The Medici who were expelled in 1494 returned in 1512 and became grand dukes; it was to Cosimo II de' Medici that Galileo dedicated his telescopic discoveries in 1610, in the same Florence whose palace still had the David at its door.

images.title: Mystic Nativity
images.caption: Botticelli's Nativity with its Greek inscription about 'the troubles of Italy' and the Book of Revelation, painted at the end of 1500 in the aftermath of the invasions and the friar's death.

images.title: Portrait of Savonarola
images.caption: A Florentine profile portrait of the friar, perhaps painted in the decades after his death, of the kind kept by his followers.

images.title: The execution of Savonarola in the Piazza della Signoria
images.caption: An anonymous Florentine painting of the execution of 23 May 1498, showing the platform, the palace and the crowd; the painting is in the Museo di San Marco. It is a later, devotional record, not an eyewitness document.
images.credit: Unknown Florentine artist; Museo di San Marco, Florence (via Bridgeman Images)

images.title: Leonardo: a palazzo and a fountain of Neptune
images.caption: A later sheet by Leonardo in which the Neptune figure is closely based on Michelangelo's David, evidence of how the statue he had helped to site stayed in his mind.
images.credit: Leonardo da Vinci; Royal Collection Trust

images.title: Agostino Vespucci's note in Cicero
images.caption: Heidelberg University's account of the marginal note dated October 1503 that names Lisa del Giocondo and Leonardo's coming council-hall commission.

images.title: Michelangelo, letter to his father Ludovico
images.caption: A letter in Michelangelo's hand from the Archivio Buonarroti (AB IV 1); his letters home are the main first-person record of his working life.

vantage_key: 0 = the principal makers and owners (the friar, the sculptor, the Opera); 1 = in the room or the Piazza (diarist, committee members); 2 = in the city but at one remove (chancery, the painter's household); 3 = elsewhere in Italy, writing later; 4 = abroad, news only.
